title: The Revolt of "Mother"
focus: a wife's quiet rebellion for a decent home

teacherSummary.text: For forty years Sarah Penn has waited for the new house her husband Adoniram promised. Instead he builds another barn. While he is away buying a horse, she moves the family and furniture into the new barn and makes it a home. Adoniram returns, is stunned, and weeps, saying he will put up partitions and windows: he never knew she was so set on it.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this story is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “The Revolt of "Mother",” how does Freeman show a wife's quiet rebellion for a decent home? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In The Revolt of "Mother", how does Freeman develop the idea of a wife's quiet rebellion for a decent home? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the characterization in the story helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how The Revolt of "Mother" develops the idea of a wife's quiet rebellion for a decent home. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and conflict shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of The Revolt of "Mother" (where it begins, turns and ends) and its characterization shape the reader's understanding of a wife's quiet rebellion for a decent home. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what The Revolt of "Mother" suggests about a wife's quiet rebellion for a decent home. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the story's characterization and conflict), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Mary E. Wilkins Freeman uses characterization in The Revolt of "Mother" to complicate the reader's understanding of a wife's quiet rebellion for a decent home. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate The Revolt of "Mother" within its historical and literary context and argue how the story's treatment of a wife's quiet rebellion for a decent home responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read The Revolt of "Mother" alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the story's handling of a wife's quiet rebellion for a decent home follows or bends those conventions, using the characterization as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to The Revolt of "Mother" and its treatment of a wife's quiet rebellion for a decent home. State your method, show what it reveals in the story's characterization and conflict, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads The Revolt of "Mother" as evidence for a larger claim about a wife's quiet rebellion for a decent home in The Revolt of "Mother". Connect close reading of the story to the whole story, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads The Revolt of "Mother" as a hinge in the story's larger treatment of a wife's quiet rebellion for a decent home. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on The Revolt of "Mother".

satQuestions.passage: Sarah Penn's face as she rolled her pies had that expression of meek vigor which might have characterized one of the New Testament saints. She was making mince-pies. Her husband, Adoniram Penn, liked them better than any other kind. She baked twice a week. Adoniram often liked a piece of pie between meals. She hurried this morning. It had been later than usual when she began, and she wanted to have a pie baked for dinner. However deep a resentment she might be forced to hold against her husband, she would never fail in sedulous attention to his wants.

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: How can someone stand up for themselves without shouting? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board. Before we start, a content note: Nothing in this story needs a special warning.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are sedulous, scuttled, inspecting, mumbled, cambric. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check the definition. Here is the first: “However deep a resentment she might be forced to hold against her husband, she would never fail in sedulous attention to his wants.” In this sentence it means: careful and persistent. Word histories: For the other words, look up the word history (Etymonline or the OED) and record the language of origin and the root meaning in your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of The Revolt of "Mother" would have known. Published in Harper's Bazar in 1890. Freeman wrote about rural New England, where farm wives had little legal say over property. Why does this story matter? A regionalist story about a woman's independence; often paired with A Jury of Her Peers and The Story of an Hour. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for characterization.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. The passage opens: “Sarah Penn's face as she rolled her pies had that expression of meek vigor which might have characterized one of the New Testament saints.” I stop and ask: what is the author doing here, and how does it connect to a wife's quiet rebellion for a decent home? I circle “sedulous”, one of today's words, and ask why the author chose it over a plainer word. When I find characterization, I underline it and write its effect in the margin, then I check my idea against the next sentence.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for characterization.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of characterization. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: Sarah Penn's face as she rolled her pies had that expression of meek vigor which might have characterized one of the New Testament saints. She was making mince-pies. Her husband, Adoniram Penn, liked them better than any other kind. She baked twice a week. Adoniram often liked a piece of pie between meals. She hurried this morning. It had been later than usual when she began, and she wanted to have a pie baked for dinner. However deep a resentment she might be forced to hold against her husband, she would never fail in sedulous attention to his wants.

Then open your writing prompt; the app shows the level your teacher assigned (for a 9–10 class, the HS Sophomore prompt reads: Analyze how The Revolt of "Mother" develops the idea of a wife's quiet rebellion for a decent home. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and conflict shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion from the 30 tiered questions (focus set for the class level): wait time, think-pair-share on DOK 3/4, follow-up probes.
segments.script: Let's talk. We move from what happens to why it matters to whether it's right. After each question I wait before calling on anyone: think first. Our anchor question: How does this story connect to women's rights in marriage? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence, and end by writing one question of your own.

segments.activity: Story quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the story quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this story suggests about a wife's quiet rebellion for a decent home, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how characterization shapes a wife's quiet rebellion for a decent home. Tonight, read the next story and add two words to your etymology log.

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.
After each answer, use a follow-up probe before moving on; ask a second student to agree, extend or challenge.
Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.
